sources.title: Why Mud Matters

discussion.body: The climate-archive advantage is a kind of absence. Mud preserves a record precisely because so little lives in it.
Worth remembering that the exceptions are the ones that matter: worms and clams do live there, so even the mud archive has tenants.

items.title: Mud's Real Job: Housing Microbes and Keeping Old Climate Records
items.body: Mud has a public-relations problem and a serious scientific résumé. In 1970, the same year as the first Earth Day, ecologist Edward Deevey wrote that mud — the essential habitat of certain essential microorganisms — is just as important as water to the economy of this planet. As JSTOR Daily notes, he wasn't being hyperbolic; half a century later the case has only become more apparent to researchers studying muddy sediments in ponds, lakes, swamps, estuaries and oceans, where those microbes live. That alone would be a decent argument for taking mud seriously. The more surprising payoff is archival: because so few larger organisms can live in mud — worms and clams being the exceptions — it makes an excellent medium for studying past climates. The scarcity of residents is the feature, not the bug.

sources.title: Explaining Hall-effect, TMR, and other new types of "mechanical" switches

discussion.body: For most typists the premium buys a specification, not a typing experience. The subtlety in daily use is the honest headline.
Subtle in daily use isn't the same as absent. The gamer case is exactly where a theoretical edge is supposed to be worth paying for.

items.title: What You're Actually Buying in a Contactless Keyboard
items.body: The mechanical keyboard isn't always so mechanical anymore. Over the past six years, keyboards using optical, Hall-effect and other “contactless” switches have become increasingly common — and they often cost more than traditional mechanical boards, which already carry a premium over basic membrane keyboards. What does the extra money get you? Ars Technica's framing is refreshingly blunt: these designs promise theoretical advantages, particularly for gamers, but in daily use the differences can be pretty subtle. That gap between the spec sheet and your fingers is the whole story. A switch that never physically closes a contact is a real engineering change; whether it changes how you type on a Tuesday afternoon is a separate question. The guide sets out to show how the newest switches work and where their advantages and disadvantages genuinely matter, which is a more useful test than the marketing numbers.

sources.title: Canadians born abroad caught up in yearslong citizenship certificate processing delays

items.title: Canada's Citizenship Backlog Was Built by Its Own Expanded Eligibility
items.body: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada is struggling to handle a flood of citizenship applications, many of them set off by a change to federal law late last year that allows anyone who can prove they have a Canadian ancestor to apply, CBC reports. The resulting backlog is described as preventing some Canadians born abroad from coming home. The policy change widened the door; the processing machinery behind it has not kept pace, and the people stuck in the queue are the ones with the clearest claim to the outcome.

sources.title: How ‘technoference’ can disrupt parent-child connections

items.title: Technoference: Five Hours of Phone Time With a Baby in the Room
items.body: There's a name for the small, everyday technology-related interruptions that disrupt in-person interactions: “technoference.” The interesting question is what happens when the person seeking attention is a small child and the person looking at a screen is their parent. One recent US study found that parents spent an average of five hours a day on their phones while they were with their babies. That figure is an average across parents, not a claim about any particular household — but as a description of how much of the shared moment sits behind a screen, it is a striking place to start thinking about the word.

sources.title: Build Canada Homes was launched a year ago. Can it scale up fast enough to meet demand?

items.title: Build Canada Homes Has Begun About 2,000 Units in Its First Year
items.body: Build Canada Homes was set up to scale up the delivery of affordable housing, at a time when industry leaders are raising alarms about the lagging pace of housing development across the country. After a year of existence, CBC reports, the agency has begun construction on about 2,000 units. Two thousand starts is the first hard figure attached to a body whose mandate is written in ambition rather than units. A year is a short time in construction and a long time in a housing crisis, which is why the agency's second year will say more than its first. Either the pace picks up, or the distance between the promise and the pipeline becomes the story. The question CBC puts to the agency, whether it can scale fast enough to meet demand, is the right one, and one count of starts doesn't answer it.

sources.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease

items.title: A Death at a Siberian Plague Institute, With Nearly 200 Contacts Under Observation
items.body: A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia has died, and nearly 200 of her contacts are under medical observation, Deutsche Welle reports. Russian authorities are denying a link to the bacterial infection, and the United States is monitoring the situation. The denial and the monitoring address different questions. A denial speaks to origin, whether this death belongs to the disease the institute studies. Observation speaks to exposure, what happens to the people who were near her. Both are underway at once, and that coexistence is the reason to follow the story rather than conclude anything from it: putting nearly 200 people under medical watch is a precautionary public-health step, and it does not by itself classify the death.

sources.title: Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone

discussion.body: A frozen line is not a frozen war. If the drones keep changing, then the same ground is a different problem every few months for the people standing on it.
Or the technology is precisely why the line holds: when movement becomes expensive enough, both sides may stop attempting it, and the map stays put.

items.title: A 700-Mile Front That Has Barely Moved in Four Years
items.body: The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches more than 700 miles, and in four years it has barely moved, NPR reports. What straddles that line is the kill zone: ground dominated by drone technology that keeps evolving. The pairing is the interesting part. A front that doesn't shift looks like stasis, but the machines above it are being redesigned continuously, so the same strip of land is never fought quite the same way twice. Static geography, fast technology — the map holds still while everything crossing it changes.

sources.title: Trouble in Paradise: Ikarie XB 1’s Music and Sound

discussion.body: Commentary gets treated as the lesser option, but a score that stands outside the image can push against it. Music that argues with a scene can say something the scene can't say about itself.
Arguing is the easy half. The harder claim is Glass's own preference: a score fused so tightly with the image that the audience stops assigning credit and experiences one thing instead of two.

items.title: Philip Glass's Two Ways to Write Film Music
items.body: Philip Glass, as quoted in a Senses of Cinema essay on the music and sound of Ikarie XB 1, said there are two ways to compose for film: you can comment on the image, or you can make the music identical with the image. He preferred the second. The distinction is about where the score stands. Commentary sits outside the picture looking in, telling you how to read a scene, and part of its power is the room it leaves for disagreement — a sweet melody under something ugly. Identity puts the music inside the picture, so that what is seen and what is heard occupy the same register and the viewer stops separating them. The essay notes that for the Koyaanisqatsi score Glass sought a radically collaborative approach, which is the identity mode pushed about as far as it goes. The piece opens with a line from Leszek Kolakowski: nothing in the world is easier than writing utopias. Declaring a score unified with its images is, on that reading, the easy part.

sources.title: Is AI the End of Math As We Know It?

discussion.body: The weekly drumbeat over the summer is the real story. September 8 gave the trend a date and a headline, but the ground was shifting before then.
Landing as a shock isn't the same as landing as mathematics. Proofs are the beginning of a conversation, not the end of one; the test is whether anyone builds on the result.

items.title: AI Models Kept Producing Proofs of Old Conjectures. Then Came September 8.
items.body: Through the summer of 2026, Quanta Magazine reports, artificial intelligence models were offering proofs of decades-old mathematical conjectures on what seemed like a weekly basis. Then came September 8: OpenAI announced that its models had solved one of the most famous problems in mathematics. Coming after months of smaller results, the claim still landed as a shock to many, the magazine writes — sudden, almost violent, in the words of its account. One distinction is worth holding onto: the September news was a company's statement about its own models, not a result demonstrated by outsiders.

sources.title: ‘The Complete Kubrick’: How Michael Chaiken & Criterion Created The First Full Collection Of Stanley Kubrick’s Filmworks

items.title: Criterion's Complete Kubrick: All 13 Features, Three Shorts, 30 Discs
items.body: Criterion is releasing The Complete Kubrick this month — a thirty-disc collector's edition that presents, for the first time in one set, all 13 films Stanley Kubrick directed, alongside his three early short films. Every title has been given a new 4K restoration, a process overseen by veteran archivist Michael Chaiken, who also produced last year's 4K project for the label. For a director whose filmography has long been scattered, one shelf holding the entire run is its own small event.

sources.title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84

items.title: Dennis Hastert, Longest-Serving Republican House Speaker, Dies at 84
items.body: Dennis Hastert has died at 84, a coroner said Monday. NPR reports that his political legacy as Congress's longest-serving Republican speaker of the House was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach.

sources.title: Israel's mental health crisis in the wake of Oct. 7 attacks

items.title: Three Years After October 7, More Than a Third of Israelis Show Symptoms, a Report Finds
items.body: Three years after the October 7 attack, Israel's health system is still struggling to come to terms with its effects, Deutsche Welle reports. A report cited in that coverage found that more than a third of Israelis have shown symptoms of mental health conditions — a figure that speaks to the scale a health system is left facing long after the immediate emergency.

sources.title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests

items.title: Sánchez Says Spain Will Vote on 29 November After Defeats on Housing Measures
items.body: Pedro Sánchez says Spain will head to the polls on 29 November, the BBC reports. The date follows recent defeats on measures aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis. Housing is the trigger, and now the campaign. An election called after those defeats moves the argument to a bigger arena: either voters hand back what the defeated measures could not win, or the same verdict arrives at national scale.

sources.title: Building advertising for the way people use AI

items.title: OpenAI Adds a Visual Ad Format to ChatGPT
items.body: OpenAI says it is introducing a new visual ad format in ChatGPT and expanding measurement tools, attribution partnerships and brand-suitability controls for advertisers. Treat this as the company describing its own product: it is an announcement of what OpenAI is launching, not an independent finding about how the ads perform. The direction of travel is the interesting part. ChatGPT gets a format advertisers can buy against, and the attribution and measurement work is the plumbing that turns a sponsored slot into something a buyer can report on — the thing every ad platform is asked for before budgets move.

sources.title: New Skydance Sets Executive Structure As Paramount-WBD Merger Set To Close

discussion.body: The load-bearing word in that report is 'simply'. Merged companies often end up wearing a hyphenated name that flatters both sides' egos; here one side's name survives alone, which is its own small statement about who won the year of politicking.

A name is the cheapest thing to settle. What Deadline's lede is really about is who runs the place, and the appointments — Casey Bloys as co-chair among them — are where the actual power sits. Those are the arrangements that took a year of negotiations and false starts to reach.

items.title: The Combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Company Will Be Called Simply Skydance
items.body: After a year of negotiations, false starts and internal and external politicking, Deadline reports, the question of who will run the media and entertainment giant created by Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. has been answered. The combined company will be called simply Skydance, and top roles have been set, including Casey Bloys as co-chair. Deadline frames the naming and the appointments as anticipated. The tell is the missing hyphen: merged companies are frequently burdened with both names, and this one carries a single one.

sources.title: Trial to start where former UBC professor alleges defamation

items.title: Steven Galloway's Defamation Trial Is Expected to Begin Monday in B.C.
items.body: A trial is expected to start Monday in B.C. Supreme Court, where Global News reports that Steven Galloway, an author and former professor, says he was defamed by accusations of sexual assault. His position is that the accusations were false; the trial is where a court weighs whether they were defamatory.

sources.title: France’s Canal+ Threatens to Pull $1.1 Billion Cinema Deal Over French Tax Hike

discussion.body: A threat to walk away is itself a bargaining chip. A €1 billion commitment is only worth honoring if the deal still makes sense after the tax change, so read the warning as a price rather than a decision.
Or it is not a bluff at all. If the investment case was built around the reduced rate, scrapping that rate is not a negotiating tactic but a change in the terms the money was promised under.

items.title: Canal+ Warns It Could Walk From a €1 Billion French Film Deal Over a VAT Increase
items.body: Canal+ Group chairman Maxime Saada has warned that the pay-TV banner could pull out of its €1 billion ($1.1 billion) investment deal with the French film industry if the government goes ahead with plans to double VAT on pay-TV subscriptions. The proposal sits in the government's proposed finance bill and would scrap the reduced 10% rate. It is a clean illustration of how much French film financing rides on tax policy rather than ticket sales alone: change how subscriptions are taxed, and an investor's answer is a threat to take a billion euros of production money elsewhere. A chairman's public warning is also a negotiating position, and the number that matters here may not be the €1 billion but the rate the government wants to double.

sources.title: Oscars: Syria Selects Doc ‘The Other Side of the Sun’ for International Feature Race, Marking First Entry Since Fall of Assad Regime

items.title: Syria's First Oscar Candidate Since Assad's Fall Is a Berlinale Documentary
items.body: Syria has chosen Tawfik Sabouni's documentary “The Other Side of the Sun” to represent it in the best international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards, Variety reports. The film had its world premiere in the Panorama section of this year's Berlinale. Variety describes it as Syria's first Oscar candidate since the fall of Syrian dictator Bashar Assad. A documentary that debuted in a festival sidebar now carries a country's banner into awards season, which is a reminder of how much of a national cinema's visibility abroad runs through festival programmers long before any distributor gets involved.

sources.title: Trial set to begin for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport

items.title: A Trial Opens in Brampton Over One of Canada's Largest Gold Heists
items.body: A man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history is set to face trial starting Monday in Brampton, Ont., Global News reports. The wording is worth keeping straight as the case moves into court: the scale of the heist, as described, comes from the investigators who worked it rather than from a finding, and “one of the largest” leaves room for cases bigger than this one. Superlatives attached to a police account and superlatives confirmed by a courtroom are not the same thing, and only one of them is at issue now.

sources.title: Jeffries says House Democrats aiming to repeat 2018 sweep by flipping Trump districts

discussion.body: Going on offense in the other party's districts is the oldest line in midterm coverage. The harder half of the story is the other one: whether a red-state sprint actually turns out voters the Democrats need to stay home.

Both camps are competing for the same scarce thing: attention. The map only widens if one side's voters lose interest, which makes the district list and the rally schedule two versions of a single bet.

items.title: House Democrats Court Republican Districts While Trump Works His Base
items.body: The Democratic Party is trying to expand the map by going on offense in Republican-held districts, while President Donald Trump is making a red-state sprint aimed at boosting voter enthusiasm and shoring up support from his base, PBS NewsHour reports. That is two theories of a campaign in one paragraph: one side bets that seats held by the other party are winnable, the other bets that the decisive variable is how many of its own voters show up. The two are not mutually exclusive, but the emphasis says where each side thinks the election is settled.
